section.title: The Weak and the Strong
section.sectionRationale: Having called the church to love one another and to put on Christ, Paul now turns to a concrete threat to that love: disputes over food and holy days between believers of tender and of robust conscience. He refuses to let secondary matters divide those Christ has welcomed. The one who eats all things must not despise, the one who abstains must not judge, for each belongs to the Lord and each will stand before God's judgment seat. The chapter reframes Christian freedom under the higher law of love that will not wound a brother for whom Christ died.
section.thesis: In matters of conscience that Scripture leaves open, believers are to welcome one another rather than despise or judge, for each of us belongs to and answers to the Lord; and love will gladly limit its own liberty rather than place a stumbling block before a brother for whom Christ died.
section.frameNote: Four movements: do not judge the servant of another, for each stands or falls to his own Master; we will all give account at God's judgment seat; do not by your eating destroy a brother, for the kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit; and act from faith, for whatever is not from faith is sin.

units.label: Welcome the weak, do not judge the Master's servant
units.note: to his own master he stands or falls

verses.text: {{proslambano|Accept}} him whose faith is {{asthenes|weak}}, without passing judgment on his opinions.
For one person has faith to eat all things, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables.
The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him.
Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.
He who observes a special day does so to the Lord; he who eats does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.

units.label: We belong to the Lord and will give account to Him
units.note: we will all stand before God's judgment seat

verses.text: For none of us lives to himself alone, and none of us dies to himself alone.
If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.
For this reason Christ died and returned to life, that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.
Why, then, do you {{krino|judge}} your brother? Or why do you belittle your brother? For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat.
It is written: “As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God.”
So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.

units.label: Do not destroy a brother for whom Christ died
units.note: the kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit

verses.text: Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any {{skandalon|stumbling block}} or obstacle in your brother’s way.
I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean.
If your brother is distressed by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. Do not by your eating destroy your brother, for whom Christ died.
Do not allow what you consider good, then, to be spoken of as evil.
For the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
For whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by men.

units.label: Pursue peace, and act from faith
units.note: whatever is not from faith is sin

verses.text: So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification.
Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All food is clean, but it is wrong for a man to let his eating be a stumbling block.
It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.
Keep your belief about such matters between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.
But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.

proslambano.gloss: To receive, welcome, take to oneself. It is a warm word, used of taking someone in as a guest or a friend. Paul commands the church to welcome the believer of tender conscience fully and gladly, not on probation, because God Himself has already welcomed him. The same welcome will be grounded in chapter fifteen in the way Christ welcomed us.

asthenes.gloss: Weak, without strength, feeble. Here it describes not weak faith in Christ but a faith not yet strong enough to be free in matters of food and days; the conscience is tender and easily wounded. Paul never mocks such a believer but calls the strong to bear with him gently, since he too is one for whom Christ died.

krino.gloss: To judge, to pass verdict, to condemn. Paul forbids believers from setting themselves up as judges over a brother in disputable matters, because there is one Judge before whose seat we will all stand. To usurp God's bench is to forget that the one you judge is the Lord's servant, not yours.

skandalon.gloss: A trap or snare, the trigger stick of a snare, hence a stumbling block that causes another to fall. Love refuses to lay such a trap in a brother's path. The strong may be free to eat, but they are not free to wield that freedom in a way that wounds a weaker conscience and trips a fellow believer into sin.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, reign, the rule of God. Paul insists the kingdom of God is not measured by what we eat or drink but by righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. To divide the church over food is to mistake the whole nature of God's reign, which is a matter of the Spirit's fruit, not of dietary rules.

basic.context: Paul turns from the great themes of the letter to a very practical problem in the Roman church. Some believers, likely with a Jewish background or scruples carried over from pagan temple practice, felt they could only eat vegetables and must keep certain holy days. Others knew they were free to eat anything. The two groups were despising and judging each other. Paul does not settle the menu; he settles the attitude. Welcome one another, because God has welcomed each of you.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter is about matters Scripture leaves open, disputable things, not the core of the gospel. Paul is not soft on truth; in Galatians he fought to the death over the gospel itself. But food and days are not the gospel, and here he pleads for patience and love. Read it as a manual for how a church holds together strong and tender consciences without either side ruining the other.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul says proslambano, welcome, the one who is asthenes, weak in faith. He forbids us to krino, to judge, a brother who is the Lord's own servant. He warns against laying a skandalon, a stumbling block, in his path. And he reminds us that the basileia, the kingdom of God, is not food and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
basic.typology: The clean and unclean foods of the law pointed forward to a deeper cleanness. Now that Christ has come and declared all foods clean, the shadow gives way to the substance. The weak believer still living among the shadows is to be treated tenderly, for the law was a guardian until Christ, and the freedom the strong enjoy is the freedom Christ purchased.
basic.christ: Christ is Lord of the living and the dead; He died and rose again precisely to be our Master, so that whether we live or die we belong to Him. The brother we are tempted to despise is one for whom Christ died. To wound him carelessly is to trample the value Christ placed on him at the cross. Christ's lordship and Christ's death together dismantle our judging.
basic.god: God has welcomed both the strong and the weak, so who are we to reject whom He receives? He is the one Judge before whose seat every knee will bow and every tongue confess. Because God alone judges the heart, we are freed from playing judge and freed to serve one another in love. His kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 7 records Jesus declaring all foods clean. First Corinthians 8 and 10 handle the same question of food and a weaker brother's conscience. Colossians 2 warns against letting anyone judge us over food, drink, or festivals, which were a shadow of Christ. Isaiah 45 stands behind the vow that every knee will bow.
basic.oneStory: The gospel that justifies the ungodly by faith also gathers strong and weak into one family. The clean and unclean laws that once marked Israel off have done their work and pointed to Christ. Now, in Him, the dividing line is erased, and the one story of God moves toward a kingdom where a countless people from every conscience and nation bow before the one Lord.

context.literary:
Romans 14:1 to 15:13 is one sustained appeal, and Paul builds it as a ring. It opens with a command to take someone to yourself, 14:1, and closes with the same verb pointed at everyone, 15:7. Between those bookends the argument runs on a chain of reasons, nearly every sentence hooked to the one before by a small 'for'. Verses 1 to 4 say whom God has received. Verses 5 to 9 say whose servants we are. Verses 10 to 12 say before whom we will stand. Only then, in verse 13, does the word 'therefore' turn the reasoning into a command: stop judging, and decide something else instead.

The verb 'judge' does the stitching. It appears in 14:3, 4, 5, 10, 13 and 22 and 23 in various forms, and Paul plays on it in verse 13, where the same root is used twice with two meanings: stop passing verdicts on one another, and pass a verdict on yourself that you will never put a trap in a brother's path. That is wordplay with a point. The energy that went into condemning is redirected into self-restraint.

The chapter is also built as two paired warnings, one for each camp. The one who eats everything is told not to despise, and the one who abstains is told not to condemn, 14:3. Later the weight shifts. From verse 13 onward nearly every instruction falls on the free, because they hold the power to wound. Paul writes the way a good pastor does, saying a short word to the sensitive and a long one to the confident.

The unit sits where the letter's great themes turn practical. Chapters 12 and 13 taught love as the shape of life under mercy, and 13:8 to 10 named love as the fulfilment of the law. Chapter 14 is that principle tested on a live wire. It then closes inside 15:1 to 13, where the argument rises into worship.
context.historical:
The disagreement did not begin in Rome. It travelled with the people. Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, a decision Luke mentions in Acts 18:2. Those who came back after his death in AD 54 returned to churches that had grown up without them and were now shaped largely by Gentile believers. Paul probably wrote from Corinth around AD 57, during the three months Luke describes in Acts 20:2 to 3, which fits the personal names in chapter 16.

Why vegetables? Several pressures could have produced it. A believer from a Jewish background in a city full of markets could not easily be sure which meat had been slaughtered by Jewish rules, or whether it had been offered to an idol first. Eating only vegetables kept the conscience clean. The pattern has a famous precedent in Daniel, who asked for vegetables and water rather than the king's food in Daniel 1:8 to 16, and who did so inside a pagan court. Wine is a different matter. Nothing in the law bans it for ordinary Israelites, so the abstainer of 14:21 may be guarding against the same worry about libations poured to idols, or may simply be an ascetic by temperament.

The days are harder to pin down. Sabbaths, new moons and annual festivals were the obvious candidates for a Jewish believer, and Paul groups the same trio with food in Colossians 2:16. But the Greek world had its own lucky and unlucky days, and fasts were also held on set days. Paul does not say, and the silence is deliberate. He is dealing with a conviction held in good faith, whatever its source.

Behind the whole scene stands the council of Acts 15. It had settled that Gentiles were not under circumcision, yet it asked them to abstain from food offered to idols, Acts 15:29. The question had been answered for the church's doctrine. It had not been answered for the church's table, which is where Romans 14 steps in.
context.canonical:
The Torah's own food laws were a sign of separation, set out in Leviticus 11, and they were meant to teach Israel to tell holy from common. Genesis 9:3 shows that the permission to eat had once been wider, 'Everything that lives and moves will be food for you', so the restriction was a chapter in the story rather than its first page. The Gospels then move the line. Mark 7:19 closes Jesus' teaching on defilement with the note 'Thus all foods are clean', and Acts 10 shows how slowly even an apostle took it in. Peter protests that he has never eaten anything unclean, and hears the answer, 'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean', Acts 10:14 and 15. Paul's own position in 14:14 and 14:20 stands on that ground.

The letter then sits beside three other Pauline texts. First Corinthians 8 and 10 handle the same question in a Greek city, where meat from the temple was the problem, and add that all food belongs to the Lord, 1 Corinthians 10:26. Colossians 2:16 to 23 shows the other edge: when food rules are urged as a way to be holier, they become a regulation of human invention and the verdict changes. First Timothy 4:3 to 5 and Titus 1:15 repeat that creation is good when received with thanks.

Philippians 2:9 to 11 takes the oath of Isaiah 45:23, which Paul quotes in Romans 14:11, and gives it to Christ. Paul reads the oath as a declaration of the same Lord who is spoken of in verses 8 and 9. Church history has used the chapter as a rule for things indifferent: what Scripture neither commands nor forbids may be left to conscience, within the limits of love.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul does not want the Romans to win an argument. He wants them to see their neighbour differently. He therefore gives no ruling on whether meat or vegetables are better, and no calendar of approved days, because the answer to that would have settled only one decade's quarrel. He gives them a way of looking: every member of the church is a servant with a Master who is able to keep that servant standing, 14:4, and every one of them will give an account to that same Master, 14:12. A person who holds those two thoughts cannot easily play judge.

He also wants the confident to hear that knowledge alone is not the finish line. He says plainly that he shares their view, 'I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself', 14:14, so no one may read him as a hesitant legalist. Then he adds that conviction does not cancel love. The freedom is real, and it is also on loan from a Christ who gave Himself.

For the hesitant, the message is quieter but just as firm. Their scruple is honoured, their liberty to hold it is defended, and they are told that God, not the stronger believer, is the one who will make them stand. What he asks of them is to stop treating a difference of practice as a difference of faith.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Paul describes two particular disagreements, food and days, and he prescribes a method for any like them. The method has four parts: welcome without arguing over opinions, 14:1; act from your own conviction, 14:5; do nothing that would lead another to violate his conscience, 14:13 and 21; and aim at what builds up, 14:19. Applying it takes judgment. A disputable matter is one where faithful Christians have read Scripture honestly and landed in different places, not one on which the apostles have spoken with a clear command.

It does not mean that anything goes. Paul himself condemns sexual sin, idolatry and false teaching without hesitation elsewhere, and in Romans 16:17 he tells the church to turn away from those who create divisions against the teaching they received. The chapter is about conscience over indifferent things, not about the gospel itself. The test question to put to a modern dispute is whether it involves what Christ has plainly commanded or only what believers have inferred.

The chapter also does not say the weak should stay weak. Paul calls them weak in faith, 14:1, which assumes growth is wanted, yet he does not ask the strong to push them there. The growth is God's work.

debates.question: Who are the weak, and what did they hold?

views.label: Jewish believers keeping Torah food and calendar rules
views.case: Most older commentators read the weak as Jewish Christians still observing dietary laws and festivals. The passage speaks of 'unclean' food, using the word common in Jewish purity talk, 14:14, and of days, which fits Sabbath and feasts. Paul's talk of the 'strong' bearing with them in 15:1 fits a Gentile majority and a Jewish minority, and 15:8 and 9 speaks directly of Jew and Gentile.

views.label: A mixed group with scruples from several sources
views.case: Others point out that no Torah law forbids all meat or all wine for ordinary Israelites, so the vegetarian and abstainer of 14:2 and 21 are not simply observing Moses. They suggest a blend: some from Jewish fear of unclean or idol-tainted meat, some from ascetic or philosophical habit, some from pagan background. Paul never names the party, which they take as proof that the principle matters more than the profile.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the weak are believers God has accepted, 14:3, and that their scruple is real. Whatever the identity, the rule is the same: welcome, do not judge, do not wound.

debates.question: Does 'one day above another' include the weekly Sabbath?

views.label: Yes, the Sabbath is among the days left to conscience
views.case: Some read 14:5 and Colossians 2:16 together and conclude that the Mosaic Sabbath, as a shadow, is no longer binding on the conscience, so a believer may treat it as special or treat every day alike. They stress that Paul says nothing to prefer one view and that Galatians 4:10 treats the keeping of special days as a danger only when it is thought to add to Christ.

views.label: No, Paul means festivals and fast days, and the Sabbath stands as a creation gift
views.case: The Reformed confessions in particular hold that the day of rest rests on creation, Genesis 2:2 to 3, and on Christ's resurrection day, and that Paul here addresses ceremonial holy days and fasts. They note that Paul does not use the word 'sabbath' in this chapter.

debates.bearing: Neither side finds a command in this chapter to defend. Where good people differ, Paul's rule is that each be convinced in his own mind, 14:5, and that nobody despise or condemn the other.

debates.question: Is the strong believer ever obliged to give up a lawful practice?

views.label: Yes, in the presence of a brother who would be led to violate his conscience
views.case: Paul's own examples in 14:15, 14:21 and 1 Corinthians 8:13 show restraint. He says he would never eat meat again if it caused a brother to fall. The chapter ties this to love, not to law.

views.label: No, to yield to every objection would hand the church to its most anxious member
views.case: Some warn that Paul also resists the demand that his own freedom be ruled by another's conscience, 1 Corinthians 10:29, and refused to circumcise Titus when the issue became a test of the gospel, Galatians 2:3 to 5. Restraint is a gift, not a surrender to pressure.

debates.bearing: The two fit together. Paul yields when the brother is genuinely at risk of being wounded and no truth of the gospel is at stake. He holds firm when someone demands compliance as a condition of acceptance.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 asks Paul's readers not to pass judgment on 'opinions'. The Greek is diakriseis dialogismon, literally a sorting out of reasonings, a phrase for the kind of argument that settles into verdicts. The command is not to welcome a person in order to start a debate. The first word, proslambano, is in the middle voice, which means take to yourself. Verse 3 uses the same verb of God, who has taken the weaker believer to Himself, and 15:7 uses it of Christ taking us.

In verse 5 the instruction 'each one should be fully convinced' translates plerophoreo, to fill to the brim. Paul uses it of Abraham, who was 'fully persuaded' that God could do what He had promised, Romans 4:21. Conviction in this chapter is therefore a settled fullness, not a nervous guess, and what Paul asks of each believer is to reach it for himself and not to borrow another's.

In verse 14 the word for 'unclean' is koinos, which means common, shared, profane. It is the word Peter uses in Acts 10:14. A thing becomes koinos not by its nature but by being counted common by the person who holds it. Paul then switches in verse 20 to a different word, katharos, clean, 'All food is clean'. So the argument is that things are clean in themselves while a person's regard for them can make them common for that person.

In verse 13 he calls what we must avoid a proskomma, from a verb meaning to strike against, a thing you trip over, and a skandalon, the trigger of a trap. The two words belong together and describe the same hazard from two angles, the accident and the snare.

Verses 15 and 20 give two strong verbs for what carelessness does. In verse 15 the word is apollymi, the verb of ruin that Jesus uses of the lost sheep. In verse 20 it is katalyo, to pull down, the word used of taking apart a building. The second is paired with 'the work of God', and the image changes from a person who perishes to a house that is demolished. Between them, Paul pictures the careless eater as both wrecker and killer, on a charge so heavy that he speaks of a brother 'for whom Christ died'.

Verse 15 also says that the eater is 'no longer acting in love'. The Greek has him no longer walking kata agapen, according to love. The verb is the ordinary one for daily conduct, so love is the road the strong believer is meant to be on, not a gesture made on the way.

Finally, in verses 22 and 23 the phrase 'from faith', ek pisteos, carries an odd sense. Here faith means conviction that an act is acceptable to God. The act that is not from faith is sin because it violates one's own persuasion, which is why the verse cannot be quoted as a general definition of unbelief.

typology.type: The clean and unclean foods of Leviticus 11
typology.fulfillment: Israel's table was a classroom. Eating the clean and refusing the unclean taught the nation that God had set them apart and that holiness reaches the most ordinary acts. The pattern ends where Jesus ends it: He declares all foods clean, Mark 7:19, and a vision to Peter turns that teaching into a mission to the Gentiles, Acts 10:15. The type is then carried upward into the new covenant, where the purity that counts is of the heart, Titus 1:15. It falls short because meat could never cleanse a conscience. Hebrews 9:9 and 10 say the old regulations of food and drink were imposed until the time of reformation, and the cleansing they pictured is provided only in Christ.

typology.type: Holy days as shadows of the things to come
typology.fulfillment: Sabbaths, new moons and feasts marked time for Israel and rehearsed what God had done and would do. Paul calls them 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ', Colossians 2:17. The Passover finds its answer in 'Christ our Passover lamb', 1 Corinthians 5:7, and the rest of the Sabbath in the rest Christ gives, Matthew 11:28 and Hebrews 4:9. In Romans 14:5 Paul does not abolish the shadows by decree; he lets each believer treat the day as to the Lord. The type is not exhausted, since the full rest awaits the new creation, Hebrews 4:9 to 11.

Isaiah records an oath sworn by God Himself that every knee will bow and every tongue will swear allegiance. In Isaiah the context is the Lord's claim to be the only God who saves, Isaiah 45:21 and 22. Paul quotes the oath in Romans 14:11 as a reason to stop judging, since the One before whom everyone kneels is not the neighbour. In Philippians 2:10 and 11 the same oath is given to Jesus, who is confessed as Lord to the glory of the Father. The correspondence is one of identity, not simply of echo. It still awaits its full scene, since the bowing in Philippians is described as in heaven, on earth and under the earth.

study.christ:
Christ enters this chapter at three points, and each carries weight. First, He is the Lord whose lordship makes our judging absurd. Verse 9 says He died and returned to life 'that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living'. Paul gives a purpose for the cross and the empty tomb that we do not usually put first: to establish a claim. Because He holds the living and the dead, a weaker believer is not the strong believer's servant, and the strong believer is not the weak one's master. They are both His. Paul has already said that the Lord is able to make a servant stand, 14:4, and the Lord in that sentence is Christ.

Second, He is the one whom the Roman believers will face. Where Isaiah speaks of every knee bowing before God, Paul writes in 14:10 that 'we will all stand before God's judgment seat', and in 2 Corinthians 5:10 the same seat is called the judgment seat of Christ. The Father and the Son are not set against each other here. The judge who will call every person to account is the one who loved them to the end, and the judgment of the believer is therefore not a trial of nerves but a meeting with the Friend who has already borne his guilt, Romans 8:34.

Third, He is the example and the price. 'Your brother, for whom Christ died', verse 15. The simplest argument against despising a brother is that Christ did not despise him. The cross establishes the worth of the believer we are tempted to treat as small. First John 3:16 draws the conclusion: 'we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers'. If giving up a meal looks costly, it is small beside what Christ gave up. Paul's chapter does not shout this. He simply puts the cross where an argument over food would normally stand.

Christ also reshapes what liberty is. The strong feel free because Christ has declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19. Yet He is also the one who 'did not come to be served, but to serve', Mark 10:45. The freedom He gave is the freedom to serve, and it is used rightly only when it takes the shape of His own life. This is why Paul can say in 14:17 that the kingdom is not a matter of eating and drinking, 'but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit', since all three are what Christ brings.

One caution keeps the reading honest. The chapter does not say that vegetables or Sabbaths foretell Christ in a hidden way; the typology comes from Paul's own statements elsewhere, as in Colossians 2:17. What Romans 14 offers is Christ as Lord, Judge, example and ransom, not as a code hidden in menus.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all a God who receives. Paul's reason for welcoming the weaker believer is that 'God has accepted him', 14:3. That statement sits before any claim about his maturity, his doctrine or his food. Before a believer can be strong or weak, he has been taken in, and the same acceptance has been given to the one who disagrees with him. A church that refuses someone whom God has accepted is arguing with the God it worships.

He is also a God who holds His servants. 'He will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand', 14:4. The verb of strength is turned from the strong believer's opinion onto the Lord's power. The sustaining of the weak is not left to the cleverness of the church. It is the Lord's own work, and the sentence says it plainly and then moves on, as though no one could doubt it.

He is the one Judge. Paul gives the doctrine of judgment a pastoral use: 'each of us will give an account of himself to God', 14:12. The thought is meant to lift a burden as well as to warn. If God judges, then no one else needs to, and no one can. It also gives weight to conduct, since what a believer does with a brother's conscience is something he will be asked about.

He is a God whose kingdom is not an arrangement of rules. Paul sets righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit against menus, 14:17. The three words describe a life ordered by Him, a life at peace with Him and with others, and a life with joy that the Spirit gives. Each of them is a relational word. A God whose kingdom looks like this cannot be pleased by a church that has fought over a menu and lost its peace.

He is a God who makes things clean. Paul stands on the conviction that nothing is unclean in itself, which rests on the doctrine of creation, 1 Timothy 4:4, and on the word of Jesus. Clean here means that created things are good in His hands. At the same time He honours the conscience, even a conscience that errs, because He has made persons who are meant to act from conviction. The doctrine of God that holds both together is a God of truth and of tender care.

For worship, the chapter sets two kinds of thanksgiving side by side. Verse 6 says the eater gives thanks to God and so does the abstainer. A congregation in which both can say grace over very different meals, and mean it, is a picture of the worship Paul wants. Praise is not made by agreement on details. It is made by a shared Lord, to whom both are giving thanks.

crossReferences.note: Jesus teaches that nothing entering a person from outside can defile him, and the evangelist adds that all foods are clean. Paul's confidence in Romans 14:14 and 14:20 is the apostolic form of this teaching, learned at the feet of the same Lord.

Peter, a Jewish apostle, refuses to eat what he has never eaten and is told not to call impure what God has made clean. The vision shows that even the apostles needed time to catch up with Jesus on food, which is a reason for the strong to be patient with the weak.

Paul faces the same question in Corinth with meat from the temple. He grants that food does not bring us closer to God and then says he would never eat meat again if it made a brother stumble. The chapter shows the principle of Romans 14 in his own conduct.

Paul tells the Corinthians to eat what is sold in the market without raising questions of conscience, and to refuse only when someone points out that the food was offered to idols, for the other person's sake. It shows that restraint is directed at a particular brother in a particular moment, not at everything that could possibly offend.

No one is to judge a believer over food, drink, a feast, a New Moon or a Sabbath, because these are a shadow and the body belongs to Christ. It supports Paul's refusal to let ceremonial matters set the terms of fellowship.

Daniel and his friends asked for vegetables and water in Babylon rather than defile themselves with the king's food. The story gives a respectable precedent for a believer who eats only vegetables out of conscience, and it also shows God favouring such a conviction, which explains Paul's refusal to belittle it.

God swears by Himself that every knee will bow and every tongue swear allegiance, after calling all the ends of the earth to turn to Him and be saved. Paul takes the oath as proof that every believer will give an account to the one God, and so no believer should assume that office for himself.

The same oath of Isaiah is here applied to Jesus: at His name every knee should bow, and every tongue confess that He is Lord, to the glory of the Father. It confirms that the Lord of Romans 14:9 and the God of 14:11 are honoured together.

All must appear before the judgment seat of Christ to receive their due for what they did in the body. Together with Romans 14:10, it shows that the judge who sits there is the Christ who died for His people, which is why the thought can humble without terrifying.

Paul refused to circumcise Titus when false brothers demanded it as a condition of acceptance. It balances Romans 14: he gives way to the sensitive conscience, and he stands firm against anyone who turns a custom into a requirement of the gospel.

Paul continues the argument in the next chapter by saying the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and that Christ did not please Himself. It shows that chapter 14 is not finished at verse 23; its logic reaches its climax in the example of Christ.

study.oneStory:
The question under Romans 14 is old: how do a people who share one God live together when they do not share every habit? Genesis 1 and 2 give the world to humanity as food and as home, and Genesis 9:3 widens the table. Leviticus 11 then narrows it for one nation, as a sign set in its daily meals. The story therefore holds both a wide beginning and a marked line in the middle, and Romans 14 stands at the place where the line is lifted without the table being thrown into chaos.

Behind the dietary laws lay a purpose, which was to say that Israel belonged to the Holy One and that the nations did not yet. Prophets such as Isaiah looked ahead to the day when the foreigner who joined himself to the LORD would be brought to the holy mountain and would find his offerings accepted, Isaiah 56:6 and 7. When Jesus declares all food clean and the Spirit falls on Gentiles in Acts 10, the wall that separated the table comes down. The weak and the strong of Rome are the first generation to live in that opened world, and they find that it is hard.

The chapter is therefore a window into how God teaches His people to live in a changed order. It does not erase the past, and it does not require the old pattern to end overnight. It trusts that one Lord can hold both. The final scene of Scripture gives the same picture on a larger scale. People 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and none of them is asked to prove that their upbringing was the right one. They are there because the Lamb has received them.

Until that day, every congregation is a small rehearsal. The believers who refuse to judge one another over disputable things are living in the new creation's peace before it arrives. They are also, as Paul says in 14:18, pleasing to God and approved by men, which means the world is watching a church that has learned to differ without division. In the end the one story moves toward a kingdom of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, 14:17, and a table at which no one is despised.

quiz.q: How does Paul say believers should treat the one whose faith is weak?

options.text: Welcome him without passing judgment on his opinions, because God has accepted him.
options.note: Paul commands a full welcome, since God has already welcomed him.

options.text: Tolerate him quietly while looking down on his scruples.
options.note: This at least stops short of excluding him, but Paul calls for genuine welcome, not condescension.

options.text: Exclude him until his faith becomes strong.
options.note: The command is to accept him now, not to place him on probation.

options.text: Require him to adopt the practice of the strong at once.
options.note: Paul does not command the weak to change; he commands the strong to bear with him.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say we must not judge a fellow believer in these matters?

options.text: Because he is the Lord's servant and we will all stand before God's judgment seat.
options.note: Each believer answers to his own Master, and God alone is the Judge.

options.text: Because right and wrong do not really exist in such matters.
options.note: Paul does not deny truth; he denies us the right to usurp God's bench.

options.text: Because everyone's opinion is equally valid on every subject.
options.note: The point is God's sole judgeship, not that all views are equally true.

options.text: Because judging others is simply impolite.
options.note: Judging here is far more than bad manners; it usurps the place of God, before whom each of us will give account.

quiz.q: What does Paul say the kingdom of God consists of?

options.text: Righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, not eating and drinking.
options.note: Paul lifts the church above dietary disputes to the Spirit's reign.

options.text: Careful observance of food laws and holy days.
options.note: Paul says explicitly the kingdom is not a matter of eating and drinking.

options.text: Mainly outward acts of religious devotion.
options.note: The kingdom does involve devotion to God, but Paul locates it in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Spirit, not in outward observance.

options.text: Personal freedom to do whatever one pleases.
options.note: It is righteousness and peace in the Spirit, not unbounded self-will.

quiz.q: Why should the strong be willing to limit their freedom?

options.text: So they do not by their eating destroy a brother for whom Christ died.
options.note: Love will forgo a lawful thing rather than wound one Christ died for.

options.text: Because their freedom is not really genuine.
options.note: Their freedom is real, yet it must yield in love so as not to destroy a brother for whom Christ died.

options.text: Because food and drink are inherently sinful.
options.note: Paul says all food is clean; the issue is love for the brother.

options.text: So they can earn approval from the weak.
options.note: The motive is love for the brother's good, not winning approval.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean when he says whatever is not from faith is sin?

options.text: Acting against one's conscience, without the conviction of faith, is sin.
options.note: The doubter who eats is condemned because he does not act from faith.

options.text: Only unbelievers ever commit sin.
options.note: Paul is addressing believers and the way they act within their convictions.

options.text: Every ordinary action is automatically sinful.
options.note: The point is acting against a doubting conscience, not that all action is sin.

options.text: Faith makes any action whatsoever acceptable.
options.note: Acting from faith is essential, but this does not license sin; it means acting in the settled conviction that it pleases God.

questions: Paul commands us to welcome the one whose faith is weak, just as God has welcomed him. Who in your church do you find easy to look down on, and how would God's welcome reshape the way you treat them?
We will all stand before God's judgment seat and give account of ourselves. How does remembering that God alone is the Judge free you from both judging others and fearing their judgment of you?
Paul says the brother you might wound is one for whom Christ died. How does the cross change the value you place on a fellow believer you disagree with?
The kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Where are you tempted to major on secondary matters and miss the heart of God's reign?
Whatever is not from faith is sin. Where is God calling you to act from settled conviction before Him rather than from mere pressure or doubt?

translationNotes.note: The phrase rendered without passing judgment on his opinions can also be translated without quarreling over disputable matters, as the BSB footnote notes; either way Paul forbids turning matters of conscience into occasions for dispute.
Some manuscripts add a clause about the one who does not regard the day; the sense is unchanged, that each believer acts to the Lord and gives thanks to God whether he observes a day or not.

Everything that is not from faith is sin speaks of acting against a doubting conscience; a few manuscripts place the closing doxology of Romans 16:25-27 after this verse, but the standard text keeps it at the end of the letter.
